title: Elder abuse and Adult Protective Services in New York
seoTitle: Report Elder Abuse in New York: APS, Scams, Who to Call
seoDesc: How to report elder abuse, neglect or money exploitation in New York: NYC and county Adult Protective Services, scam hotlines, the ombudsman and what APS does.
dek: If you think an older New Yorker is being hurt, neglected or cheated, you can make a report today. Here is who to call in New York City and the rest of the state, and what happens next.
keyFacts: Danger right now: call 911
NYC Adult Protective Services: 718-557-1399, weekdays 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., or 311
Statewide APS helpline: 1-844-697-3505, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 8 p.m.
APS serves adults 18+ regardless of income; NYC accepts anonymous reports
Scams: NY Attorney General helpline 1-800-771-7755
body:
If an older adult is in danger right now, call 911. For abuse, neglect or money being taken that is not an emergency, call Adult Protective Services (APS). In New York City, that is 718-557-1399. Everywhere else, it is your county Department of Social Services, or the state APS helpline at 1-844-697-3505.

You do not need proof to make a report. You only need a real concern. This guide explains who APS helps and what happens after you call. It also covers money abuse, scams and problems in nursing homes or assisted living.

Who do I call about elder abuse in New York?

SituationWho to call
Someone is in immediate danger911
Abuse, neglect or self-neglect in the five boroughsNYC APS at 718-557-1399, Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., or 311. Online at nyc.gov/apsrefer
Abuse, neglect or self-neglect elsewhere in the stateYour county Department of Social Services APS unit, or the NYS APS helpline at 1-844-697-3505, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Not sure if it is abuse and want to talk it throughElder Abuse Helpline for Concerned Persons, 844-746-6905
Domestic violence, including by a spouse or partnerNYS Domestic and Sexual Violence Hotline, 1-800-942-6906 (711 for deaf and hard of hearing callers), 24 hours
Scams and consumer fraudNY Attorney General, 1-800-771-7755
Problems in a nursing home, adult home or assisted livingLong Term Care Ombudsman Program, 1-855-582-6769

Outside the city, county APS units have their own local numbers. You can find yours through the state Office of Children and Family Services or by calling the state APS helpline above.

Who does Adult Protective Services help?

APS helps adults 18 and older, at any income level, who meet all three of these conditions.

  • They have a physical or mental impairment.
  • Because of it, they cannot manage their money, meet their daily needs or protect themselves from abuse, neglect, exploitation or other hazards without help.
  • They have no one available who is willing and able to help them responsibly.

That last point matters. If your father has a capable daughter helping, APS may decide he does not need its services. If the person hurting him is the one "helping," that person does not count.

APS also handles self-neglect. That might be an older neighbor in Yonkers who has stopped eating, is surrounded by spoiled food and will not let anyone in.

You do not need proof to call. A real worry is enough.

What happens after I make a report?

  1. Intake. A worker asks what you have seen and how to reach the person. NYC APS accepts anonymous referrals and keeps the information confidential.
  2. Screening. APS decides whether the person appears to meet the three conditions above.
  3. Home visit. In NYC, APS visits within 24 hours if the situation looks life threatening, and within three business days in other cases.
  4. Decision. After the visit, APS decides whether to open a case. Some counties, such as Tompkins, tell the person who made the report whether the case was accepted.
  5. Service plan. If the case is opened, a caseworker builds a plan with the person and checks in over time.

Can my parent say no?

Often, yes. Adults have the right to make their own choices, including choices their family disagrees with. If the person refuses help and is judged safe with the supports they have, the case may close. If the situation is unsafe, APS keeps the case open and keeps trying to engage them. Tompkins County APS explains that it cannot force treatment for mental health or substance use, unless there is an immediate danger to the person or others.

When someone truly cannot make decisions, a court may need to appoint a guardian. See our Article 81 guardianship guide.

What can APS actually do?

New York City's APS brochure lists the kinds of help a caseworker can arrange, depending on the plan.

  • Medical and psychiatric exams and ongoing care
  • Help applying for or renewing Medicaid and home care
  • Help with rent and utility arrears
  • Public assistance, SSI and SSD benefits
  • Housing Court help to prevent eviction
  • Other living arrangements
  • Managing Social Security benefits for someone who cannot
  • Referrals to the NYPD and the District Attorney for abuse or exploitation
  • Heavy-duty cleaning
  • Court petitions for a community guardian to manage financial and household affairs

Counties outside the city offer similar case management, but the details vary. Ask your county APS what it can provide.

What does financial exploitation look like?

Money abuse is often quiet. It can come from a stranger, a new "friend," a paid helper or a relative. The Department of Financial Services (DFS) lists these warning signs.

  • Unpaid bills the person should be able to pay
  • Sudden or unexplained transfers of money or property
  • Confusion about recent financial changes
  • Unusual spending
  • A new close acquaintance who seems to want access to accounts
  • Recent changes to a will, trust or insurance policy

What to do

  • Call APS if the person seems unable to protect themselves.
  • Call DFS at 1-800-342-3736. DFS says it can take complaints and investigate suspected elder financial exploitation.
  • Call local police if money was stolen.
  • Call the bank's fraud department and ask about freezing or flagging the account.

A durable power of attorney with an agent your parent trusts can prevent a lot of this. See our power of attorney guide.

Which scams target older New Yorkers?

The state Office for the Aging cites FBI figures showing adults over 60 lost more than $3.4 billion to scams in 2023. The NY Attorney General and the state Office for the Aging warn about these common ones.

  • Grandparent scam. A caller pretends to be a grandchild in trouble and begs for money, often asking you not to tell the parents.
  • Government imposters. Callers claim to be from the IRS, Medicare or Social Security. The state Office for the Aging says no federal agency will call you out of the blue like this.
  • Gift card requests. Anyone who asks you to pay with gift cards and read the numbers over the phone is running a scam.
  • Prize and sweepstakes scams. Real contests never ask for money up front.
  • Fake checks. You deposit a check, wire some back, and the check bounces later.
  • Home repair scams. Someone knocks with leftover material from a job "around the corner," or a "free inspection" finds costly problems.
  • Tech support scams. A pop-up says the computer is infected and gives a number to call. Never let a stranger take remote control.
  • Romance scams. A new online love interest who needs money.
  • Parcel and phishing texts. Messages about a missed delivery or a locked account that ask for personal details.

Where to report a scam

  • NY Attorney General helpline: 1-800-771-7755 (deaf or hard of hearing: 1-800-788-9898), or online at ag.ny.gov/file-complaint
  • Federal Trade Commission: reportfraud.ftc.gov
  • FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center: ic3.gov
  • Local police, using 911 to file a report
A simple family rule

Agree that no one in the family sends money because of a call, text or email without first hanging up and calling back on a number you already know. The Attorney General advises hanging up and contacting the company yourself.

Who helps people in nursing homes and assisted living?

The Long Term Care Ombudsman Program advocates for residents of nursing homes, assisted living and other licensed adult care homes. Ombudsmen help resolve complaints, explain residents' rights and work with residents, families and staff. When a problem cannot be fixed that way, they can refer it to the state Department of Health or another agency.

Call 1-855-582-6769 or use the Find Your Ombudsman page. If you suspect abuse that puts a resident in danger, call 911 first. Checking a home's record before a move also helps. See our nursing home ratings guide.

What other help is there in New York City and upstate?

  • NYC Aging Elder Justice programs. Community partners in each borough offer case help, crisis intervention, safety planning, shelter referrals, counseling and help with Family, Criminal and Housing courts. Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469.
  • NYC Aging C-PASS. The Crime Prevention and Support Services program helps older adults hit by scams, theft, robbery, harassment or assault. It can help file complaints with the FTC or FBI and apply to the state Office of Victim Services for crime-related losses.
  • Upstate Elder Abuse Center at Lifespan. Call 1-866-454-5110.
  • NY Connects. For services that can lower risk, such as home care, meals and caregiver support, call 1-800-342-9871. See our caregiver support guide.

How to stay calm and helpful

  • Write down what you saw, with dates. Keep copies of odd bank statements or letters.
  • Talk to your parent alone, in a quiet moment. Ask open questions and listen.
  • Do not confront a suspected abuser in a way that could put your parent at more risk.
  • Make the report, then keep visiting and calling. Staying close helps protect your parent.

faq.q: How do I report that my mom is being taken advantage of in the Bronx?
faq.a: Call NYC Adult Protective Services at 718-557-1399, Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., call 311, or refer online at nyc.gov/apsrefer. If money was stolen, also call the police. If she is in danger right now, call 911.

faq.q: Who do I call about my dad being neglected by a caregiver in Syracuse?
faq.a: Call Onondaga County's Adult Protective Services unit, or the state APS helpline at 1-844-697-3505, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. If he is in immediate danger, call 911.

faq.q: Can I report elder abuse anonymously in New York?
faq.a: Yes. New York City APS accepts anonymous referrals and keeps the information confidential. Outside the city, county APS units such as Tompkins County's keep the caller's identity confidential unless you want the person to know.

faq.q: Does Adult Protective Services cost money or have an income limit?
faq.a: APS serves adults 18 and older regardless of income. Eligibility depends on having an impairment, being unable to protect themselves or manage daily needs, and having no one willing and able to help.

faq.q: Can APS remove my parent from their home?
faq.a: APS works to help people stay safely at home and adults can usually refuse services. If someone cannot make decisions and is at risk, a court may appoint a guardian, which is a separate legal process.

faq.q: Where do I report a scam call targeting an older adult in New York?
faq.a: Call the NY Attorney General's helpline at 1-800-771-7755 or file online at ag.ny.gov/file-complaint. You can also report to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov and to the FBI at ic3.gov.

sources: NYSOFA: Elder Abuse Prevention and Interventions
Tompkins County DSS: APS frequently asked questions
NYS Long Term Care Ombudsman Program
NYC Aging: Elder Abuse and Crime

title: Help for family caregivers in New York: respite, leave and support
seoTitle: Help for Family Caregivers in New York (2026 Guide)
seoDesc: Where New York family caregivers get help: county Offices for the Aging, NYC Aging, respite, dementia support, Paid Family Leave figures and tax credits.
dek: New York has free counseling, respite, dementia support and paid leave for people caring for an older relative. Here is where to start, who qualifies and what each program pays.
keyFacts: Start with NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871, or Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 in NYC
Family caregiver support covers adults caring for someone 60+, or anyone with dementia
NY Paid Family Leave pays 67% of your average weekly wage for up to 12 weeks
PFL weekly maximum is $1,228.53 in 2026 and $1,287.91 for leave starting in 2027
NY's child and dependent care credit can cover care for a disabled spouse or adult dependent
body:
If you are helping a parent or spouse with bills, meals, rides or personal care, New York has help for you. Your first call is NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871, or Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 if your loved one lives in one of the five boroughs.

The state says 4.1 million New Yorkers take on a caregiving role each year, giving more than 2.6 billion hours of hands-on care. Many of them never call it caregiving. This guide covers the free support programs, respite, dementia help, Paid Family Leave and the tax credits that can ease the cost.

Where does a family caregiver in New York start?

Caregiver help in New York runs through the local Area Agency on Aging. Outside New York City, that is your county Office for the Aging (some counties use a slightly different name). Inside the city, it is NYC Aging, the city's Department for the Aging.

  • Outside NYC: Call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871. It routes you to the county where your loved one lives, which matters more than where you live.
  • In the Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens or Staten Island: Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 (212-AGING-NYC), Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.

You do not need to live with the person you care for. New York's Caregiver Resource Centers serve family members and other informal caregivers whether or not they live together. That helps if you live in Albany and your dad lives in Binghamton.

Call the county where your parent lives, even if you live somewhere else.

The state also runs a free online Caregiver Portal at newyork-caregivers.com, with free resources and training for unpaid caregivers. Read more about the front door to services in our guide to NY Connects.

What does the National Family Caregiver Support Program offer?

The National Family Caregiver Support Program (NFCSP) is a federal program under the Older Americans Act. In New York, county Offices for the Aging and NYC Aging run it. It pays for services aimed at the caregiver, so you are the client.

Who can get NFCSP helpDetails
Caregiver of an older adultAdult relative or other unpaid caregiver of someone 60 or older
Dementia caregiverAdult caregiver of someone of any age with Alzheimer's disease or a related disorder
Grandparents and other relatives raising childrenNon-parent relatives 55 or older raising a child under 18
Older parents of adults with disabilitiesRelatives 55 or older, including parents, caring for an adult 18 to 59 with a disability

The program offers five kinds of help.

  • Information about services near you.
  • Help getting connected, including applying for benefits.
  • Counseling, support groups and training, so you can make care decisions and solve problems with less guesswork.
  • Respite, meaning short breaks while someone else provides care.
  • Supplemental services on a limited basis. In New York these can include home-delivered meals, personal emergency response buttons, minor home changes, assistive devices and legal services.

Funding is limited and every county sets its own mix. Ask what is available now, how long the wait is and if there is a suggested contribution.

What help is there for caregivers in New York City?

NYC Aging estimates there are 1.3 million family caregivers in the city. Its caregiver programs work through community partners in every borough. They offer:

  • Information, referrals and long-term care planning
  • Support groups and one-on-one counseling
  • Caregiver training
  • Respite care
  • Help applying for benefits
  • Limited financial assistance

Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 and say you are a caregiver. They will match you with the caregiver program that covers your loved one's community district. The NYC Aging caregiving page also has a Service Finder to locate programs near you.

NYC Aging funds some social adult day programs too. These give your parent supervision, meals and activities during the day, and give you predictable time off. Most centers are private and are paid by Medicaid or by the family, so ask about cost before you visit.

How do I get a break from caregiving?

Respite is short-term care so you can rest, work, see a doctor yourself or travel. It can be a few hours of in-home help, a day program or an overnight stay. A planned break is easier to arrange than an emergency one, so ask early.

Here are the main routes to respite in New York.

  • NFCSP respite through the county Office for the Aging or NYC Aging, for the caregivers listed above. In NYC this can include in-home day or night care, adult day services or an overnight stay in a nursing home.
  • EISEP respite. The state's in-home program for people 60+ who are not on Medicaid includes respite for family caregivers outside of a nursing home or other facility. See our EISEP guide.
  • Dementia respite through the state's regional Alzheimer's caregiver programs (see below).
  • Medicaid home care. If your parent has Medicaid, home care hours may let you step back. Some families use the consumer directed program so a relative can be paid as the aide. See our CDPAP guide and Medicaid guide.

Questions to ask when you call

  • Is there a waiting list for respite, and how long is it?
  • How many hours could we get, and how often?
  • Is there a cost share or a suggested contribution?
  • Can respite happen at home, or only at a day program or facility?
  • Do you have support groups at times I can attend, in person or by video?

What help is there for dementia caregivers?

The New York State Department of Health funds three statewide Alzheimer's programs. It calls this a $25 million annual investment in community support and health services.

ProgramWhat it offers
Alzheimer's Disease Regional Caregiver Support InitiativeTen regional organizations offering caregiver assessments, support groups, education, wellness programs and respite care
Alzheimer's Disease Community Assistance ProgramRun by Alzheimer's Association chapters, with a 24-hour helpline at 800-272-3900 for information and referrals
Centers of Excellence for Alzheimer's DiseaseTen regional centers that diagnose and manage dementia and refer families to community support

To find the providers for your parent's county, use the Health Department's county program list. In New York City, NYC Aging's caregiver programs also serve caregivers of people of any age with Alzheimer's disease or a related disorder.

If you are early in the dementia journey, a Center of Excellence visit can confirm the diagnosis and give you a plan. It is also a good time to sign a health care proxy and a power of attorney while your parent can still do so.

Can I get paid leave from work to care for a parent?

Yes, if you work for a private employer in New York. New York Paid Family Leave (PFL) gives job-protected, paid time off to care for a family member with a serious health condition. Workers pay for it through a small payroll deduction.

Paid Family Leave2026Leave starting in 2027
Benefit67% of your average weekly wage, up to the cap
Maximum weekly benefit$1,228.53$1,287.91
NY State Average Weekly Wage$1,833.63$1,922.25
LengthUp to 12 weeks
Employee contribution0.432% of gross wages, up to $411.91 a year0.452% of gross wages, up to $451.81 a year

The state puts the maximum total benefit for leave starting in 2027 at $15,454.92, which is 12 weeks at the top weekly rate.

Who counts as family?

You can take PFL to care for a spouse, domestic partner, child or stepchild, parent or stepparent, parent-in-law, grandparent, grandchild or sibling. The family member can live outside New York. So a daughter in Rochester can take leave to help her mother after surgery in Florida.

Am I eligible?

  • If you work 20 or more hours a week, you qualify after 26 consecutive weeks with your employer.
  • If you work under 20 hours a week, you qualify after 175 days worked, which do not need to be in a row.
  • Citizenship and immigration status do not affect eligibility.

You can take leave all at once or in full-day pieces. Someone who works three days a week, for example, can take up to 36 separate days.

How to apply

  1. Tell your employer. Give at least 30 days' notice if the leave is foreseeable, or as soon as you can if it is not.
  2. Get the forms. You need the Request for Paid Family Leave (PFL-1) and the Health Care Provider Certification (PFL-4). Your parent signs a release (PFL-3) and gives it to their doctor. The PFL-3 does not go to the insurer.
  3. Fill in your parts. Give the PFL-1 to your employer, who must return it within three business days. Have your parent's doctor complete their part of the PFL-4.
  4. Send everything to your employer's insurance carrier. Mail or fax the forms within 30 days after your leave begins.
  5. Call the helpline if you get stuck. The PFL Helpline is 844-337-6303, Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

If you work for a government employer, ask human resources if you are covered. The full rules are at paidfamilyleave.ny.gov.

What tax help is there for caregivers in New York?

New York has no general tax credit just for being a family caregiver. Two state credits can still help, depending on your situation.

  • Child and dependent care credit. It is not only for children. It can cover care for a disabled spouse who cannot care for themselves. It can also cover another disabled person who cannot care for themselves, lived with you more than half the year and is your dependent. You must qualify for the federal credit first. For full-year residents, the state credit is fully refundable. The separate New York City credit only covers care for a child under 4, so it does not apply to care for a parent or spouse. See the Tax Department's credit page.
  • Long-term care insurance credit. If you pay premiums on a qualifying long-term care policy, the state gives a nonrefundable credit of 20% of the premiums paid that year. For individuals, it is capped at $1,500 and is limited to people with New York adjusted gross income under $250,000. It is claimed on Form IT-249. See the credit page.

Federal rules on claiming a parent as a dependent and deducting medical costs are separate. A tax preparer, or a free volunteer tax site, can check what fits your family.

What mistakes do new caregivers make?

  • Waiting for a crisis. Many programs have waiting lists. Call after the first fall or the first scary forgetful moment, before a hospital stay forces your hand.
  • Calling the wrong county. Services follow the person receiving care. Call the office where your parent lives.
  • Skipping the legal papers. Without a health care proxy and power of attorney, you may face a court case later. See our guardianship guide for what that involves.
  • Not telling your employer. PFL has a notice rule and a 30-day window to file. Missing either can delay your pay.
  • Doing it all alone. More than half of unpaid caregivers in New York do not see themselves as caregivers, according to the state. Saying the word out loud on the phone opens doors.
After a hospital stay

Ask the hospital discharge planner for a referral to your county Office for the Aging or NYC Aging before your parent leaves. A case manager can start the paperwork for home care, meals and respite while you focus on the trip home.

faq.q: How do I get help caring for my mom in Queens?
faq.a: Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 and say you are a family caregiver. NYC Aging will connect you with the caregiver program for your mom's community district, which can offer counseling, support groups, training, respite and benefits help.

faq.q: Can I get paid to take time off to care for my dad in Buffalo?
faq.a: If you work for a private employer in New York, Paid Family Leave can pay you 67% of your average weekly wage for up to 12 weeks. The cap is $1,228.53 a week in 2026 and $1,287.91 for leave starting in 2027. Your dad can live anywhere, including out of state.

faq.q: Who runs caregiver support outside New York City?
faq.a: Each county Office for the Aging runs the National Family Caregiver Support Program and other services. Call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 to reach the office in the county where your loved one lives.

faq.q: Is there help for caregivers of someone with dementia in New York?
faq.a: Yes. The state Health Department funds regional caregiver support programs with assessments, support groups, education and respite. There is also a 24-hour Alzheimer's Association helpline at 800-272-3900.

faq.q: Can I take Paid Family Leave a day at a time?
faq.a: Yes. PFL can be taken in full-day increments instead of all at once. The number of days depends on how many days a week you usually work, so a three-day-a-week worker can take up to 36 days.

faq.q: Does New York have a tax credit for family caregivers?
faq.a: There is no general caregiver credit. The state child and dependent care credit can cover care for a disabled spouse or adult dependent who lived with you more than half the year. The long-term care insurance credit is 20% of qualifying premiums, up to $1,500.

title: EISEP in New York: home care for older adults not on Medicaid
seoTitle: EISEP in New York: Who Qualifies and How to Apply
seoDesc: EISEP pays for home care for New Yorkers 60+ who are not on Medicaid. Who qualifies, the cost share, services, waiting lists and how to apply in NYC and beyond.
dek: The Expanded In-home Services for the Elderly Program helps New Yorkers 60 and older who need help at home but do not qualify for Medicaid. Here is who gets it, what it costs and how to apply.
keyFacts: For New Yorkers 60+ who need help with 1 daily activity or 2 household tasks
Not for people eligible for the same services through Medicaid
No cost share at or below 150% of the federal poverty level
Full cost at or above 250% of poverty, sliding scale in between
Apply through your county Office for the Aging, NY Connects (1-800-342-9871) or Aging Connect (212-244-6469)
body:
EISEP pays for help at home for New Yorkers 60 and older who need a hand with daily tasks but are not on Medicaid. You apply through your county Office for the Aging, or through NYC Aging if you live in the five boroughs.

The full name is the Expanded In-home Services for the Elderly Program. It began in 1987. It fills the gap for older adults who have too much income or savings for Medicaid but cannot easily pay a home care agency's full rate. This guide covers who qualifies, what it pays for, the cost share and how to get on the list.

What is EISEP?

EISEP is a state program run locally by Area Agencies on Aging. Outside New York City, that means your county Office for the Aging. In the city, NYC Aging runs it through community case management agencies.

Every EISEP client gets a trained case manager. That person visits, assesses what help is needed, sets up services and checks in over time. The case manager can also connect you to other help, such as home-delivered meals or benefits screening.

EISEP is not an entitlement. It runs on a yearly state budget amount plus federal and local money, and each local Area Agency on Aging must put in a 25% local match. When the money for the year is committed, new clients may wait.

EISEP is for the parent who is too comfortable for Medicaid and too strapped for full-price home care.

The state Office for the Aging testified to the State Assembly in October 2024. It said 10,585 people were getting personal care through these programs from all funding sources. The average client was 82 to 83 years old.

Who qualifies for EISEP?

RequirementRule
Age60 or older
NeedHelp with at least one activity of daily living (such as bathing or dressing) or two instrumental activities (such as housekeeping, cooking or shopping)
SafetyCan be kept safely at home with the help
MedicaidNot eligible for the same services through Medicaid
IncomeNo income limit to apply, but income sets your cost share

The Medicaid rule is the one that trips families up. If your parent looks eligible for Medicaid, the county will usually steer them to Medicaid home care instead. Some counties, such as Onondaga, also say people who qualify for VA-funded home care are not eligible. In NYC, the rule is that a client cannot be eligible for aide or housekeeping services through another government program, including Medicaid or Medicare.

Examples of what counts as a need

  • Activities of daily living: bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, moving from bed to chair, eating.
  • Instrumental activities: light housekeeping, laundry, meal preparation, shopping, errands.

Say your mother in Schenectady can bathe and dress on her own, but since her hip replacement she cannot vacuum, carry laundry or shop. That is two instrumental activities, which can be enough to qualify.

What services can EISEP pay for?

  • Case management. Assessment, a care plan, follow-up and connection to other community services.
  • Personal Care Level I. Housekeeping, cooking, shopping and similar household tasks.
  • Personal Care Level II. Hands-on help with activities of daily living, such as bathing, dressing and grooming.
  • Consumer directed in-home services. In some counties, the client hires and directs their own aide. The state reported almost 1,000 people in 42 counties using this option in 2024.
  • Respite for family caregivers. A break for the caregiver that does not involve a stay in a nursing home or other facility.
  • Ancillary services. Goods and services that help someone stay home, such as minor home repairs, assistive devices or personal items.

How aides are hired varies by county. Some counties use licensed home care agencies. Others hire aides directly. The state said 14 Area Agencies on Aging had started hiring aides directly or working with one agency exclusively.

Hour limits in New York City

NYC Aging's home care standards cap service at 8 hours a week for clients who only need housekeeping, and 20 hours a week for clients who need personal care and housekeeping. The case management agency can add hours for special situations, such as an escort to a doctor's appointment. Counties outside the city set their own limits, so ask yours.

How much does EISEP cost?

Some clients pay nothing. Others pay part or all of the cost, based on income compared with the federal poverty level.

Household incomeWhat the client pays
At or below 150% of the federal poverty levelNo cost share
Between 150% and 250% of povertyA share of the cost on a sliding scale
At or above 250% of povertyThe full cost of services

In Onondaga County, for example, clients below the cost share threshold do not have to pay but may contribute if they are able. The county says about 40% of its clients fall below that line. Ask your county how it sets the sliding scale.

Your case manager will do a financial review at the first visit. Have these ready:

  • Social Security and pension award letters
  • Recent bank statements
  • Rent, mortgage, property tax and utility costs
  • Health insurance cards and a medication list

In NYC, a client who will not share financial information must agree to pay the maximum cost share. If you disagree with the cost share, a denial or a discharge, you have the right to ask for a hearing. You can ask out loud or in writing, within 30 days of getting the notice.

How do I apply for EISEP?

  1. Call the right office. Outside NYC, call your county Office for the Aging or NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871. In the five boroughs, call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 (212-AGING-NYC), Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., and ask for a home care assessment.
  2. Answer the screening questions. Expect questions about age, health, what your parent can and cannot do, current help and income.
  3. Have the home visit. A case manager assesses needs, reviews finances and takes a health and social history. Be honest about the hard days, not only the good ones.
  4. Get a care plan. The case manager authorizes a number of hours a week and explains the cost share.
  5. Services begin. In NYC, city standards say the home care program should start services within five business days of getting the referral.
  6. Stay in touch. The case manager keeps in contact and reassesses over time. Onondaga, for example, asks clients to check in by phone every two months and does a home reassessment each year.

If your parent already has some home care and needs more, Aging Connect and the county office can help with that too.

What if there is a waiting list?

Waiting lists are common because funding is set each year and aides are hard to find. In NYC, if fewer hours are available than were approved, a program can start with fewer hours when that is safe. The client stays on a wait list for the rest.

While you wait:

  • Ask where your parent stands on the list and when to call back.
  • Tell the case manager right away if things get worse, such as a fall or a hospital stay. The case manager may need to reassess.
  • Ask about other help in the meantime, like home-delivered meals, a day program or caregiver respite.
  • Check Medicaid eligibility again if your parent's savings are dropping. See our Medicaid guide.
  • Look at private care. Our home care agencies guide explains licenses and what to ask.

When does Medicaid home care make more sense?

EISEP is for people who are not Medicaid eligible. If your parent qualifies for Medicaid, Medicaid home care is the route to use. In some cases it can also pay a family member through the consumer directed program. See our CDPAP guide.

For some families, a PACE program may also fit. See our PACE guide. NY Connects can compare options with you in one call.

Trust and safety at home

Any aide coming into the home should come through the county, NYC Aging's contracted agency or a licensed home care agency. Do not leave cash, checkbooks or jewelry out, and tell the case manager right away if anything feels wrong.

What mistakes should families avoid?

  • Assuming you earn too much. There is no income cap to apply. Higher income means a higher cost share, but case management still helps.
  • Waiting until after a crisis. Getting on a list early can mean help arrives when you need it.
  • Calling the county where you live. Call the office where your parent lives.
  • Downplaying needs at the assessment. Many older adults put on a brave face for visitors. Ask to sit in.
  • Missing the hearing deadline. If services are denied, ended or the cost share looks wrong, ask for a hearing within 30 days of the notice.

faq.q: How do I get home care for my dad in Brooklyn if he is not on Medicaid?
faq.a: Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469. NYC Aging will refer him to a local case management agency, which assesses his needs and decides whether he qualifies for city-funded home care for people 60 and older who are not eligible for Medicaid home care.

faq.q: My mom lives in Westchester and needs help with housework. Can EISEP help?
faq.a: Possibly. EISEP covers people 60 and older who need help with at least two household tasks, like cleaning and shopping, or one personal care task. Call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 to reach the Area Agency on Aging in Westchester County and request an assessment.

faq.q: Is there an income limit for EISEP?
faq.a: There is no income limit to apply. Income sets the cost share. People at or below 150% of the federal poverty level pay nothing, those between 150% and 250% pay on a sliding scale, and those at or above 250% pay the full cost.

faq.q: Can someone on Medicaid get EISEP?
faq.a: No. EISEP is for older adults who are not eligible for the same services through Medicaid. If your parent qualifies for Medicaid, the county will usually point you to Medicaid home care instead.

faq.q: How many hours of help does EISEP give?
faq.a: It depends on the assessment and the county. In New York City, the limit is 8 hours a week for housekeeping only, and 20 hours a week for personal care plus housekeeping, with extra hours possible for special situations.

faq.q: What can I do if EISEP denies or ends services?
faq.a: You have the right to a hearing on a denial, a disputed cost share or an involuntary discharge. Ask for it out loud or in writing within 30 days of receiving the notice.

NYSOFA: EISEP testimony to the Assembly Committee on Aging (Oct 2024)
NYSOFA: EISEP and CSE client rights to a hearing
NYC 311: Home care for older adults
NYC Aging: Home Care Program Standards

title: Article 81 guardianship in New York: when it's needed, how it works
seoTitle: Article 81 Guardianship in New York, Step by Step
seoDesc: How Article 81 guardianship works in New York: who can petition, court fees, the court evaluator, the 28-day hearing, reports and less restrictive options.
dek: When a parent can no longer manage money or care decisions and never signed a power of attorney, a court may need to appoint a guardian. Here is how New York's Article 81 process works.
keyFacts: Filed in Supreme Court or County Court under Mental Hygiene Law Article 81
Hearing within 28 days of the judge signing the order to show cause
Court fees: $210 index number, $95 request for judicial intervention
Guardian's initial report is due within 90 days of the commission
Free help for family guardians: the courts' Guardian Assistance Network
body:
Article 81 guardianship is a New York court case in which a judge decides whether an adult is incapacitated and, if so, appoints a guardian with only the powers that person needs. It is usually the route families take when a parent can no longer manage money or personal decisions and never signed a power of attorney or health care proxy.

It is a serious step. A guardianship takes away some of a person's legal rights, so the law sets a high bar and requires a hearing. This guide explains when it's needed, how to start a case, what it costs in court fees, and the less drastic options to try first.

When is a guardian needed?

A New York judge can appoint a guardian only if the person is likely to suffer harm because they can't care for their property or personal needs and can't adequately understand the consequences. The law calls this person the alleged incapacitated person, or AIP, until the judge decides.

The person asking for the guardian must prove incapacity by clear and convincing evidence. That is a higher standard than in most civil cases.

A judge can appoint a guardian for two kinds of needs, or both.

  • Personal needs. Making health care decisions, deciding where the person lives, applying for benefits and getting confidential records.
  • Property management. Paying bills, organizing assets, signing contracts and, with permission, making gifts.

The judge's order lists exactly which decisions the guardian may make and which the person keeps. The law requires the least restrictive form of intervention. So a parent who can still decide where to live, but can't handle a brokerage account, may get a guardian for property only.

Try the alternatives first

Before appointing a guardian, the court must look at whether other resources already meet the person's needs. Article 81 lists examples: visiting nurses, home health aides, adult day care, senior centers, powers of attorney, health care proxies, trusts, and representative or protective payees.

What are the less restrictive alternatives?

If your parent can still understand and sign documents, the simplest path is to have them sign planning papers now.

  • A power of attorney covers money and property. See our guide to powers of attorney in New York.
  • A health care proxy names someone to make medical decisions. See health care proxy and MOLST in New York.
  • A representative payee, appointed by Social Security, can manage Social Security or SSI checks.
  • A trust can hold assets and name a trustee to manage them.

Services can also reduce the need for a guardian. Home care, adult day programs and help from the county Office for the Aging may let a parent stay safe without a court order. Our guide to caregiver support in New York lists where to start.

Guardianship tends to become necessary when a parent has already lost capacity, refuses help while in danger, is being exploited, or has no valid documents and a bank or nursing home needs someone with legal authority.

Who can file, and in which court?

Article 81 cases are heard in Supreme Court or County Court. In New York City, that means the Supreme Court in the borough where your parent lives. The law allows a petition by any of these.

  • The person themselves.
  • A presumptive distributee, meaning a close relative who would inherit if there were no will.
  • An executor, administrator or trustee connected to the person.
  • The person they live with.
  • Anyone otherwise concerned with their welfare, which can include a public agency such as the county Department of Social Services.
  • The head of a hospital, nursing home or other facility where the person is a patient or resident.

The case starts with an order to show cause and a verified petition with supporting papers. The petition explains why a guardian is needed, what powers are requested and who should serve.

How does the case move forward?

  1. Prepare the papers. Draft the order to show cause and verified petition with facts about your parent's condition, finances and current supports. Most families use a lawyer for this.
  2. File and pay fees. Buy an index number and file a request for judicial intervention with the county clerk and court.
  3. The judge signs the order to show cause. This sets the hearing date and usually appoints a court evaluator.
  4. Serve the papers. Your parent and others entitled to notice must be served as the order directs.
  5. The court evaluator investigates. The evaluator meets your parent, looks into the claims and writes a report for the judge.
  6. The hearing. It must take place no more than 28 days after the judge signs the order to show cause. The judge hears testimony and decides.
  7. The guardian qualifies. If appointed, the guardian takes an oath, files any required bond and receives a commission, the document that proves their authority.

What does the court evaluator do?

The court evaluator is the judge's eyes and ears. The evaluator may be a lawyer, physician, psychologist, accountant, social worker, nurse or another trained person. They must speak with your parent, investigate the petition and file a written report.

The court may also appoint a lawyer for your parent, and in some situations the law requires it. Before the hearing, a judge can appoint a temporary guardian if there's an urgent need.

What does guardianship cost?

Court filing fees are set by state law and are the same in every county's Supreme Court.

CostAmount or rule
Index number$210
Request for judicial intervention$95
Motion or cross-motion$45 each
Court evaluator, if guardian appointedReasonable fee set by the court, paid from your parent's estate
Court evaluator, if petition denied or dismissedCourt may order the petitioner, your parent, or both to pay

The bigger costs are usually lawyers' fees for the petitioner, the court evaluator's fee, and any lawyer appointed for your parent. A guardian may also need a bond, which carries a premium. None of these has a fixed state price, so ask your lawyer for a written estimate of the whole case before filing.

In the five boroughs, NYC Aging funds free legal services for residents 60 and older, and guardianship is one of the listed areas. Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469. Elsewhere, call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 to ask your county Office for the Aging about legal programs.

The fees add up, which is one more reason to get a power of attorney and health care proxy signed while a parent can still sign.

What does a guardian have to do after appointment?

Being a guardian is ongoing work with court oversight.

  • Training. Article 81 sets education requirements for guardians. The initial report must include proof of guardianship training.
  • Initial report. Due within 90 days of receiving the commission. It describes the steps you've taken, and it includes a property inventory and a personal needs plan where those fit the powers you were given.
  • Annual report. Filed every year in May, unless the court orders otherwise. It includes a financial accounting and a summary of your parent's health and living situation.
  • Court examiner review. The annual report is filed with the clerk of the court that appointed you, and a copy goes to the court examiner, who examines the reports. Keep receipts and bank records from day one.

Where can a family guardian get free help?

The New York State courts run the Guardian Assistance Network, started in April 2005. It gives free help to family guardians appointed under Article 81 anywhere in the state. Staff work one on one with lay guardians on their required reports. It offers online training that satisfies the court-ordered training requirement. It does not give legal advice. Learn more on the Guardian Assistance Network page.

What should families know before filing?

Talk with your parent first if you can, and with siblings. Contested guardianships take longer and cost more. A family meeting may surface a simpler fix, or at least agreement on who should serve.

Gather facts the court will want. That means a list of doctors, medications and diagnoses, a picture of bank accounts, income and bills, and examples of the harm or risk you're worried about. Be specific. "Mom missed three months of rent and gave $8,000 to a caller claiming to be her grandson" carries more weight than "Mom is confused."

If you suspect a parent is being financially exploited or neglected right now, don't wait for a guardianship case. Call Adult Protective Services. Our Adult Protective Services guide explains how. APS can act quickly and, in some cases, may petition for a guardian itself.

faq.q: How do I become guardian for my dad in the Bronx?
faq.a: You file an Article 81 petition in the Bronx County Supreme Court, starting with an order to show cause and verified petition. The judge sets a hearing within 28 days of signing the order and usually appoints a court evaluator. NYC residents 60 and older can get free legal help, including on guardianship, through Aging Connect at 212-244-6469.

faq.q: How long does an Article 81 guardianship take in New York?
faq.a: The hearing must be held no more than 28 days after the judge signs the order to show cause. Preparing the papers beforehand, and the guardian qualifying afterward, add time. Contested cases usually take longer.

faq.q: Do I need guardianship if my mom in Westchester already has a power of attorney?
faq.a: Often not. The court must consider whether existing resources such as a power of attorney and health care proxy already meet her needs. A guardian may still be needed if the documents don't cover a problem, or if she is in danger and refusing help.

faq.q: What are the court fees for guardianship in New York?
faq.a: In Supreme Court, the index number is $210 and the request for judicial intervention is $95, with $45 for each motion. Lawyer, court evaluator and bond costs are separate and usually larger.

faq.q: When is the guardian's annual report due in New York?
faq.a: Every guardian must file a report annually in May, unless the court orders otherwise. The initial report is due within 90 days of receiving the commission.

faq.q: Is there free help for family members who become guardians?
faq.a: Yes. The New York courts' Guardian Assistance Network gives free help to family guardians statewide, including one-on-one help with required reports and online training that meets the court-ordered requirement. It does not give legal advice.

sources: NY CourtHelp, what happens after an Article 81 case is filed

title: Health care proxy, living will and MOLST in New York
seoTitle: Health Care Proxy and MOLST in New York
seoDesc: New York's health care proxy needs two adult witnesses, no notary. Learn how living wills, the Family Health Care Decisions Act, MOLST and DNR orders work.
dek: How to sign New York's health care proxy, what a living will adds, who decides when there is no proxy, and how MOLST orders work for people who are seriously ill.
keyFacts: New York's health care proxy needs two adult witnesses. No lawyer or notary is required.
Your agent or alternate agent cannot sign as a witness.
With no proxy, the surrogate order is spouse or domestic partner, adult child, parent, adult sibling, then close friend.
MOLST (DOH-5003) is signed by a physician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant and reviewed at least every 90 days.
Photocopies, faxes and scans of a signed MOLST are valid, and it does not need to be pink.
body:
A health care proxy is the one form every adult in New York should sign. It names a health care agent to make medical decisions if you can no longer make them, and it needs only two adult witnesses, with no lawyer or notary.

A living will adds written instructions. A MOLST is different again. It is a set of doctor's orders for people who are already seriously ill. This guide explains each one, what New York law does if there is no proxy, and where to get the official forms free from the Department of Health (DOH).

What is a health care proxy in New York?

It is a short legal form that lets you appoint a health care agent, someone you trust to speak for you with doctors. DOH says everyone over 18 should have one. The agent steps in only when and if a doctor decides you cannot make your own decisions. Until then, you decide.

Your agent can make all health care decisions for you, or only the ones you list. They must decide based on your wishes, or on your best interests if your wishes are not known. Any adult 18 or older can be your agent. You can also name an alternate, who acts if your first choice is not available.

A health care proxy is separate from a power of attorney. A power of attorney covers money and property. A proxy covers medical care. Most people need both. See our guide to the power of attorney in New York.

How do I fill out New York's health care proxy form?

Download the New York State Health Care Proxy form from health.ny.gov. It is one page plus instructions, and DOH offers the instructions in several languages. The Attorney General notes you do not have to use that exact form.

  1. Pick your agent. Choose someone who will follow your wishes even if they would choose differently. Ask them first.
  2. Pick an alternate. Name a second person in case the first cannot be reached.
  3. Write any limits or wishes. You can add instructions in the space provided. If you have views on feeding tubes or IV fluids, write them down or tell your agent clearly. Without a clear sense of your wishes, your agent cannot decide about artificial nutrition and hydration.
  4. Sign in front of two witnesses. Both must be 18 or older. Your agent and alternate cannot sign as witnesses.
  5. Fill in the organ donation section if you want to. Have that section witnessed by two people too. Leaving it blank does not mean you refuse to donate.
  6. Hand out copies. Give copies to your agent, your doctor and anyone else you choose. Keep one with your important papers and bring one to any hospital stay, even outpatient surgery.

You can cancel a proxy by telling your agent or your health care provider, out loud or in writing. If you name your spouse and later divorce or legally separate, your former spouse can no longer act as your agent unless the form says otherwise.

Two adult witnesses, no notary, no lawyer. Most families can finish this at the kitchen table.

Does New York have a living will?

A living will is a written statement of specific treatment wishes, such as if you would want a breathing machine if you were permanently unconscious. DOH says it can be part of your health care proxy or a separate document.

The proxy is usually the stronger tool. A living will cannot answer questions you did not think of. An agent can. Many people write a few lines of wishes on the proxy form itself, then talk them through with their agent. Talk early, before a hospital stay.

What happens if my parent has no health care proxy?

New York's Family Health Care Decisions Act (FHCDA) lets a family member or close friend act as a surrogate. It was signed in March 2010, and nursing homes had to follow it by June 1, 2010. It covers decisions in hospitals, nursing homes and hospice programs.

The surrogate is the first available person on this list, in this order.

PriorityWho can be the surrogate
1Spouse (if not legally separated) or domestic partner
2An adult son or daughter, 18 or older
3A parent
4An adult brother or sister, 18 or older
5A close friend who has kept in regular contact and gives the doctor a signed statement

If a court has already appointed a legal guardian, the guardian can make these decisions. The surrogate must follow the patient's known wishes, or their best interests when wishes are not known. For stopping life-sustaining treatment, the law sets extra conditions. The treatment must be an extraordinary burden, and the patient must, for example, be expected to die within six months or be permanently unconscious. Every hospital, nursing home and hospice must have an ethics review committee to help settle disputes.

This works, but it is slower and less certain than a proxy. If you have three adult children who disagree, all three are at the same priority level. A higher-priority surrogate can hand the role to someone else on the list, but anyone ranked above that person can object. A signed proxy avoids all of that. If no proxy exists and big decisions about money also need to be made, see our guide to Article 81 guardianship.

What is MOLST, and how is it different from a DNR?

MOLST stands for Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment. It is New York form DOH-5003, a set of doctor's orders about CPR, breathing tubes, feeding tubes, antibiotics and hospital transfer. DOH says it is for people with serious health conditions, people who live in or need long-term care, and people who might die within the next year.

DocumentWhat it doesWho signsWhen it takes effect
Health care proxyNames your agentYou, plus two adult witnessesWhen a doctor says you cannot decide
Living willWritten treatment wishesYouWhen you cannot speak for yourself
MOLST (DOH-5003)Medical orders on CPR, intubation and other treatmentPhysician, nurse practitioner or physician assistant, with consent from the patient or decision-makerAs soon as it is signed
Nonhospital DNR (DOH-3474)Order not to resuscitate outside a hospitalPhysician, nurse practitioner or physician assistantAs soon as it is signed

A DNR order covers only one thing, CPR. A MOLST covers CPR and much more. Under state law, MOLST is the only form in New York that can record both a nonhospital do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order and a do-not-intubate (DNI) order. Emergency crews, home care agencies, hospices, hospitals and nursing homes must honor it. A MOLST does not replace a proxy. Your parent should have both.

A few practical points from the DOH MOLST FAQ.

  • The form does not have to be on pink paper. Pink is easier to spot in an emergency, but white is valid.
  • Photocopies, faxes and scans of a signed form are valid.
  • At home, keep it on the refrigerator, by the phone in the kitchen or at the bedside.
  • The clinician must review it at least every 90 days, and after a move, a major change in health or a change of mind.
  • DOH announced a revised form in May 2025 (the current form is dated 06/25). Older versions are still valid.

What is eMOLST?

eMOLST is the electronic version of the MOLST form. Clinicians complete it on a computer instead of on paper. When DOH revised the paper form in 2025, the electronic version was updated to match. DOH also said the eMOLST registry, run by Excellus, is no longer taking new provider applications, though providers with an existing agreement can keep using it.

For families, the takeaway is simple. Paper or online, ask for a printed copy of your parent's MOLST, keep it where DOH advises and bring it to every new hospital, nursing home or hospice.

Where do I get the forms, and what should I do next?

All of these are free from DOH. You do not need to buy a kit.

  • Health care proxy. Form and instructions on the DOH health care proxy page. The New York Attorney General links to the form and explains it in plain language.
  • MOLST. The DOH-5003 form and guidance are on the DOH MOLST page. Your parent fills it out with a doctor, nurse practitioner or physician assistant, never alone.
  • Decision guide. DOH's Deciding About Health Care explains proxies, surrogates and DNR orders for patients and families.

Say your mom lives in Syracuse and you live in Albany. Get her proxy signed on your next visit, with two neighbors as witnesses. Put a copy in her doctor's chart and keep one on your phone. If she has a serious illness, ask her doctor about MOLST at the next appointment. These steps take an afternoon and save a lot of guessing in an emergency room.

Related guides: hospice care in New York and support for family caregivers.

faq.q: How do I get my dad to sign a health care proxy in Nassau County?
faq.a: Print the free New York State Health Care Proxy form from health.ny.gov. He names an agent and an alternate, then signs in front of two adults who are not the agent or alternate. No lawyer or notary is needed. Give copies to his doctor and his agent.

faq.q: My mom is in a nursing home in the Bronx and has no proxy. Who makes medical decisions?
faq.a: Under the Family Health Care Decisions Act, a surrogate decides. A legal guardian can decide if one has been appointed. Otherwise it is the first available person in this order: spouse or domestic partner, an adult child, a parent, an adult sibling, then a close friend. The surrogate must follow her known wishes or her best interests.

faq.q: Does a New York health care proxy need to be notarized?
faq.a: No. New York's form needs only two witnesses who are 18 or older. Your agent and alternate agent cannot be witnesses.

faq.q: What is the difference between MOLST and a DNR?
faq.a: A DNR order covers only CPR. MOLST (form DOH-5003) is a set of medical orders covering CPR, breathing tubes and other life-sustaining treatment. It is the only form in New York that can record both a nonhospital DNR and a DNI order.

faq.q: Is a photocopy of a MOLST form valid?
faq.a: Yes. DOH says photocopies, faxes, scans and other accurate copies of a signed MOLST are valid. It does not have to be on pink paper. Stamped signatures are not allowed.

faq.q: Can I cancel or change my health care proxy?
faq.a: Yes. Tell your agent or your health care provider, out loud or in writing. Then sign a new form and give out new copies. If you named your spouse and later divorce or legally separate, they can no longer be your agent unless you said otherwise on the form.

New York State Health Care Proxy form (Publication 1430)
Deciding About Health Care: A Guide for Patients and Families (Publication 1503)
Dear Nursing Home Administrator Letter: Family Health Care Decisions Act
Health Care Proxy, New York State Attorney General
MOLST frequently asked questions, NY Department of Health
DOH announces revision of MOLST form, May 2, 2025

title: Power of attorney in New York: the form, the rules and the bank
seoTitle: New York Power of Attorney: 2021 Rules Explained
seoDesc: How New York's statutory short form power of attorney works since the 2021 changes: signing, notary, witnesses, agent duties, bank acceptance and revoking it.
dek: A power of attorney lets someone you trust handle your money and paperwork if you can't. Here is how New York's form works since the 2021 changes, and what to do when a bank pushes back.
keyFacts: New York's updated power of attorney law took effect June 13, 2021
Sign before a notary and two witnesses (the notary can be one of them)
A New York power of attorney is durable unless it says otherwise
Banks must act within 10 business days of getting the original or a certified copy
Free legal help for NYC residents 60+: Aging Connect, 212-244-6469
body:
A New York power of attorney is a signed document that names an agent to handle your financial and legal matters. To be valid it must be signed, dated, notarized and witnessed by two people, and it keeps working if you later lose capacity unless it says otherwise.

That last point is why families care so much about it. If your mom or dad signs one while they are well, you can pay their bills and talk to their bank later without going to court. If nobody signs one, the family may need a guardianship case instead. This guide covers the form, the 2021 rule changes, what an agent must do, and how to handle a bank that says no.

What is a New York statutory short form power of attorney?

New York law sets out a standard form, called the statutory short form power of attorney. It appears word for word in section 5-1513 of the General Obligations Law. The person signing is the principal. The person they choose is the agent.

The form lets the principal grant authority by subject. The subjects run from real estate and bank accounts to retirement plans, tax matters, government benefits and records. You initial the ones you want to grant. You can name more than one agent and say whether they must act together or may act separately. You can also name successor agents in case the first choice can't serve.

A power of attorney covers money and property only. The form itself says your agent cannot make health care decisions for you. For medical choices, you need a separate health care proxy. Our guide to the health care proxy and MOLST in New York explains that form.

Durable is the default

Under New York law, a power of attorney is durable unless it expressly says it ends if the principal becomes incapacitated. Durable means it keeps working after the principal loses capacity, which is the whole point for most families.

What changed in 2021?

New York rewrote its power of attorney law in Chapter 323 of the Laws of 2020, signed December 15, 2020, and then fine-tuned it in Chapter 84 of the Laws of 2021. The new rules took effect June 13, 2021, the date the General Obligations Law itself uses for the switch. Several changes made the form easier to use.

  • Substantial compliance. The old law demanded the exact statutory wording. Now the form only has to substantially conform to the statutory form. Small typos no longer sink it. Optional sections you don't use can be marked "Intentionally Omitted."
  • No more gifts rider. The separate Statutory Gifts Rider was repealed. Gift authority now goes in the Modifications section of the main form.
  • Higher small-gift limit. An agent may make gifts for personal and family maintenance of up to $5,000 total per calendar year, up from $500. Larger gifts need express authority in Modifications.
  • Two witnesses. The principal's signature must be witnessed by two people who are not named as agents or gift recipients. Under the old law, witnesses were needed only for the gifts rider.
  • Rules for banks. Banks and other third parties now have firm deadlines to accept or reject the form, and can owe damages if they refuse without good reason.

A power of attorney that was valid when it was signed under the old rules is still valid. You don't have to redo a pre-2021 form just because the law changed. Many families choose to update older forms anyway, especially if an agent has died or moved away.

How do you sign one so it holds up?

The signing rules are strict, and banks check them closely. Here they are in one place.

RequirementWhat New York law says
Principal's signatureSigned and dated by the principal while they have capacity. Another person may sign at the principal's direction, in their presence.
NotaryThe principal's signature must be acknowledged before a notary, the same way a real estate deed is.
WitnessesTwo witnesses who are not named as agents or gift recipients. The notary can serve as one of them.
Agent's signatureEach agent signs and dates the form, and the agent's signature is also notarized.
When it startsFor each agent, on the date that agent's signature is acknowledged, unless the form names a later date or event.
GiftsUp to $5,000 a year total for personal and family maintenance. More requires express authority in Modifications.
  1. Talk about the choice first. Pick an agent your parent trusts with money, and a backup. Ask the agent if they are willing.
  2. Get the current form. Use the post-2021 statutory short form. Fill in names, initial the powers granted and complete Modifications if needed.
  3. Line up a notary and two witnesses. Many banks, pharmacies and law offices have notaries. Witnesses can't be the agents or anyone getting gifts under the form.
  4. Sign with everyone present. The principal signs and dates in front of the notary and witnesses.
  5. Have the agent sign before a notary. The agent can sign later, but the power isn't effective for that agent until they do.
  6. Store the original safely. Keep it where the agent can find it. Give the agent copies, and consider an attorney-certified copy for banks.

Should it be springing or start right away?

Most New York powers of attorney start as soon as the agent signs before a notary. A springing power of attorney instead says it takes effect on a future date or when something happens, such as the principal losing capacity.

New York allows this. The law says a springing power takes effect only once the date or event in the document has occurred and the agent's signature has been notarized. The document can say that a named person, such as a doctor or a family member, must declare in writing that the event has happened. That written declaration then satisfies the requirement.

Springing powers sound appealing because nothing changes until it's needed. The trade-off is delay. At a stressful time, your family may need to get a written declaration before anyone can pay the rent. If you go this route, spell out exactly who makes the call and how.

A power of attorney works best when it's signed early, while your parent can choose freely and explain their wishes.

What does an agent have to do?

An agent is a fiduciary. That legal word means they must act in the principal's interest and put their own aside. Section 5-1505 of the General Obligations Law spells out the duties.

  • Act with the care a prudent person would use with someone else's property.
  • Follow the principal's instructions. When there are none, act in the principal's best interest.
  • Avoid conflicts of interest.
  • Keep the principal's money separate from the agent's own, except for property they already own jointly.
  • Never give the principal's property to themselves unless the form specifically allows it.
  • Keep a record of all receipts, payments and transactions.

The principal can also name a monitor, someone who can ask the agent for records. When a monitor, co-agent or certain others make a written request, the agent must hand over the records and a copy of the power of attorney within 15 days.

Agents are entitled to be reimbursed for reasonable expenses. They get paid for their time only if the principal says so in the Modifications section.

Spotting misuse

Most agents are honest family members doing their best. Still, a power of attorney gives someone broad control over money. Warning signs include unexplained withdrawals, bills going unpaid, or an agent who won't share records. If you suspect financial abuse of a parent, see our guide to Adult Protective Services in New York.

What if the bank won't accept it?

This used to be the most common complaint. Since 2021, New York sets clear deadlines for banks and other third parties.

Within 10 business days of receiving the original or an attorney-certified copy, the bank must do one of three things. It can honor the power of attorney. It can reject it in writing with its reasons. Or it can ask the agent for a sworn, notarized affidavit. If the bank rejects it and you respond, the bank has seven business days to honor it or give a final written rejection. If it asks for an affidavit, it must honor the form within seven business days of getting a proper one.

Some reasons for refusing are allowed. These include actual knowledge that the principal has died, actual knowledge of a report to Adult Protective Services, or the agent refusing to provide an original or attorney-certified copy. Other reasons are not enough on their own. A bank can't refuse just because the form isn't the bank's own form, because time has passed since it was signed, or because the agent signed on a different date than the principal.

New York law says it is unlawful to unreasonably refuse a properly signed power of attorney. The agent can bring a special court proceeding. If the court finds the refusal unreasonable, it can award damages, including reasonable attorney's fees and costs.

These deadlines do not apply to some government bodies, including public retirement systems and the agencies that run Medicaid. Those offices follow their own procedures.

How do you revoke or replace a power of attorney?

The form itself tells the principal they can revoke it at any time, for any reason, as long as they are of sound mind. Here is how it works under section 5-1511.

  • Tell the agent in writing. Deliver a signed, dated revocation in person, or send it by mail, courier, email or fax to the agent's last known address.
  • Tell the bank and others. A revocation doesn't bind a bank or other third party until it gets actual notice. Send written notice to each place the agent has used the form.
  • Record it if needed. If the power of attorney was recorded, for a real estate sale for example, record the revocation in the same office where it was recorded.
  • Say so in any new form. Signing a new power of attorney does not automatically cancel an old one. The form has a section on whether it revokes earlier ones, so fill it in deliberately.

A power of attorney also ends when the principal dies. At that point the executor named in the will takes over. Our guide to probate in New York explains that step. If the agent is the principal's spouse, the agent's authority ends on divorce or annulment unless the form says otherwise.

How much does it cost to get help?

The form is free, and some families complete it on their own. Notary fees are small. Most of the cost comes from paying a lawyer to draft it, explain the choices and supervise the signing. New York doesn't set lawyers' fees, so ask for a flat fee in writing before you start.

Free help exists for older adults. In the five boroughs, NYC Aging funds free legal services for residents 60 and older. Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 and ask for legal help. Outside New York City, many county Offices for the Aging run or fund legal programs for people 60 and older. Call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 to reach your county's office.

A lawyer is worth it if your parent owns a business or rental property, wants to allow large gifts for Medicaid planning, has a blended family, or is showing early memory loss. Those are the situations where a clear form, signed at the right time, saves the most trouble later.

faq.q: Does a New York power of attorney need two witnesses?
faq.a: Yes. Since June 13, 2021, the principal's signature must be witnessed by two people who are not named as agents or gift recipients, and it must be notarized. The notary can serve as one of the two witnesses.

faq.q: How do I get power of attorney for my mom in Brooklyn?
faq.a: Your mom has to sign it herself while she still has capacity. She signs the New York statutory short form before a notary and two witnesses, and you sign as agent before a notary. NYC residents 60 and older can get free legal help through Aging Connect at 212-244-6469. If she can no longer understand what she's signing, you may need an Article 81 guardianship instead.

faq.q: My dad's bank in Buffalo won't accept his power of attorney. What can I do?
faq.a: Under New York law the bank must accept it, reject it in writing with reasons, or ask you for a notarized agent affidavit within 10 business days of getting the original or an attorney-certified copy. Ask for the rejection in writing, fix any real problem it names, and respond. An unreasonable refusal can lead to a court proceeding where the bank may owe damages and attorney's fees.

faq.q: Is a power of attorney signed before 2021 still good in New York?
faq.a: Yes. A power of attorney that was valid when it was signed remains valid under the 2021 law. Some families update older forms anyway so banks see the current version, or because an agent has changed.

faq.q: Can a power of attorney make medical decisions in New York?
faq.a: No. The New York statutory short form covers financial and legal matters only and says the agent cannot make health care decisions. Use a separate health care proxy for medical choices.

faq.q: Does a power of attorney still work after my parent dies?
faq.a: No. It ends at death. After that, the executor named in the will, or an administrator appointed by the Surrogate's Court, handles the estate.
